topics: Causes of First-Row Anomalies (Small Size, High IE/EN, No d-Orbitals)
Maximum Covalency Rule (Period 2 Covalency Capped at 4)

Inert Pair Effect Mechanism (Reluctance of 6s² Electrons to Bond)
Heavy p-Block Oxidation State Stabilities & Redox Behavior
quickSummary: First-row elements (B, C, N, O, F) cannot expand octets due to the absence of d-orbitals. In heavy p-block (Tl, Pb, Bi), the Inert Pair Effect stabilizes lower oxidation states (Tl⁺, Pb²⁺, Bi³⁺), making PbO₂ an oxidizing agent.
summary: Master first-row element anomalies, octet expansion restrictions, diagonal relationships, and the Inert Pair Effect in heavy p-block chemistry.

conceptBreakdown.heading: 7.1 Causes of Anomalous First-Row Behavior
conceptBreakdown.title: 7.1 Causes of Anomalous First-Row Behavior

summaryBox.title: First-Row Anomalies
summaryBox.takeaway: 1. Exceptional small size; 2. High electronegativity/IE; 3. Complete absence of vacant d-orbitals (max covalency = 4, no octet expansion).

EXCEPTIONAL SMALL SIZE          HIGH ELECTRONEGATIVITY & IE    ABSENCE OF VACANT d-ORBITALS
Unusually small atomic and      Strong electron attraction;    Valence shell limited to n=2;
ionic radii; high charge/size.  high covalent character.       Maximum Covalency = 4 (2s, 2p).
conceptBreakdown.content:
• **Octet Expansion Restriction**: Heavier elements utilize vacant $d$-orbitals to expand valence shells ($\text{SF}_6, \text{PCl}_5, \text{SiF}_6^{2-}$). First-row elements lack $2d$ orbitals; their maximum covalency is capped at **4** ($\text{BF}_4^-$ exists, but $\text{BF}_6^{3-}$ and $\text{NCl}_5$ are IMPOSSIBLE).
• **$p\pi-p\pi$ Multiple Bonding**: First-row elements readily form strong $p\pi-p\pi$ bonds ($\text{C}=\text{C}, \text{N}\equiv\text{N}, \text{C}=\text{O}$). Heavier congeners overlap weakly and prefer single $\sigma$-bonds.

conceptBreakdown.heading: 7.2 Diagonal Relationships & Inert Pair Effect
conceptBreakdown.title: 7.2 Diagonal Relationships & Inert Pair Effect
conceptBreakdown.codeSnippet:
STABILITY SPECTRUM (Heavy p-Block)
                        
   GROUP 13:   Al³⁺ > Ga³⁺ > In³⁺ > Tl⁺ > Tl³⁺  (Tl⁺ is most stable)
   GROUP 14:   C⁴⁺ > Si⁴⁺ > Ge⁴⁺ > Sn⁴⁺ > Pb²⁺ > Pb⁴⁺ (Pb²⁺ is most stable)
   GROUP 15:   N⁵⁺ > P⁵⁺ > As⁵⁺ > Sb⁵⁺ > Bi³⁺ > Bi⁵⁺ (Bi³⁺ is most stable)
conceptBreakdown.content:
• **Diagonal Relationships ($\text{Li} \sim \text{Mg}, \text{Be} \sim \text{Al}, \text{B} \sim \text{Si}$)**: Arise because moving across a period increases $Z_{\text{eff}}$ while moving down a group decreases it, giving diagonal pairs almost identical ionic radii and polarising power ($\frac{\text{Charge}}{\text{Radius}^2}$).

• **Inert Pair Effect**: Intervening $4f^{14}$ and $5d^{10}$ subshells shield poorly, drawing outer $6s^2$ electrons tightly toward the nucleus so they refuse to unpair and bond:
- **Group 13**: $\text{Tl}^+$ is much more stable than $\text{Tl}^{3+}$.
- **Group 14**: $\text{Pb}^{2+}$ is much more stable than $\text{Pb}^{4+}$. (Hence $\text{PbO}_2$ is a strong oxidizing agent).
- **Group 15**: $\text{Bi}^{3+}$ is much more stable than $\text{Bi}^{5+}$.

quickRevision: Period 2 elements have max covalency = 4 (NCl₅ and BF₆³⁻ cannot exist).
Diagonal pairs: Li ~ Mg, Be ~ Al, B ~ Si.
Inert pair effect makes lower oxidation states (+1 for Tl, +2 for Pb, +3 for Bi) most stable.
PbO₂ (Pb⁴⁺) is a powerful oxidizing agent; SnCl₂ (Sn²⁺) is a strong reducing agent.
keyFormulae: Inert Pair Stability: Tl⁺ > Tl³⁺, Pb²⁺ > Pb⁴⁺, Bi³⁺ > Bi⁵⁺
